clinicalPearls: Most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, typically presenting in the second or third decade of life.

Classic presentation is episodic gross (macroscopic) hematuria occurring within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory or mucosal infection, distinguishing it from post-streptococcal GN which lags 1-3 weeks.
Can also present as asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria found incidentally on urinalysis.
Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy showing dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.
Course is highly variable: some patients have a benign lifelong course while roughly 20-40% progress to end-stage kidney disease over 20 years.
Recurrent gross hematuria episodes typically resolve completely between attacks, but persistent proteinuria or hypertension signals higher risk.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is considered a systemic variant of the same underlying disease process affecting skin, gut, and joints.
Renal biopsy findings are graded using the Oxford (MEST-C) classification to help predict prognosis and guide therapy intensity.
harrison.pathophysiology: Disease arises from circulating poorly galactosylated IgA1 molecules that form immune complexes, which deposit in the glomerular mesangium and trigger mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion. This deposition activates complement and local inflammatory pathways, leading to variable degrees of mesangial hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, endocapillary proliferation, and interstitial fibrosis depending on disease severity. Mucosal immune stimulation (e.g., respiratory infection) is thought to transiently boost production of these abnormal IgA1 complexes, explaining the synpharyngitic timing of gross hematuria flares.
additionalDifferentials: Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria)
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis with microscopy — confirms dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts indicating glomerular bleeding
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine protein — quantifies proteinuria for staging and prognosis
Serum creatinine and estimated GFR — establishes baseline kidney function and tracks progression
Serum complement levels (C3, C4) — typically normal in IgA nephropathy, helping exclude complement-mediated GN
Kidney biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy — required for definitive diagnosis and Oxford classification grading
Serum IgA level — often elevated but neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm diagnosis alone
ANA, ANCA, and hepatitis serologies — helps exclude secondary causes and mimicking systemic diseases
Renal ultrasound — assesses kidney size and excludes obstructive or structural causes of hematuria
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting crescentic (rapidly progressive) IgA nephropathy requiring urgent nephrology evaluation
Nephrotic-range proteinuria or nephrotic syndrome at presentation
New or worsening hypertension poorly responsive to therapy
Systemic features (purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain) suggesting IgA vasculitis with renal involvement
Persistent proteinuria greater than 1 gram per day despite optimized supportive therapy
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent gross hematuria solely to urologic causes and delaying nephrology referral or biopsy.
Assuming normal complement levels rule out all forms of glomerulonephritis rather than supporting IgA nephropathy specifically.
Underestimating long-term risk in patients with isolated microscopic hematuria who lack proteinuria monitoring over time.
Confusing timing of hematuria onset relative to infection with post-streptococcal GN, missing the synpharyngitic pattern typical of IgA nephropathy.
harrison.prognosis: Course ranges from indolent with preserved kidney function over decades to progressive decline, with an estimated 20-40% of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease within 20 years of diagnosis. Higher risk features include persistent proteinuria, hypertension, reduced GFR at presentation, and unfavorable histology on Oxford classification.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Glomerular Diseases (IgA Nephropathy)
management: Establish optimised supportive care as the foundation — maximally tolerated renin-angiotensin system blockade, blood pressure control, and an SGLT2 inhibitor to lower proteinuria
Reinforce lifestyle measures including dietary sodium restriction, weight management, and smoking cessation
For persistent proteinuria and high progression risk despite supportive care, consider gut-targeted enteric budesonide or a course of systemic corticosteroids weighed against toxicity
Consider newer agents such as the endothelin-angiotensin receptor antagonist sparsentan or complement-directed therapy in appropriate patients
Treat rapidly progressive crescentic disease with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide
Monitor proteinuria, blood pressure, and eGFR over time to detect progression, using the Oxford (MEST-C) biopsy classification for risk stratification
Plan kidney replacement therapy or transplantation for those progressing to kidney failure, counselling on post-transplant recurrence
